name: Jacques Laffitte

summary.text: Jacques Laffitte (1767–1844) was a Paris banker and politician. In 1825, after Haiti accepted Charles X's ordinance requiring a 150-million-franc indemnity, the Haitian government borrowed 30 million francs on the Paris market to make the first instalment; the bank Ternaux et Gandolphe prepared the loan and a syndicate led by Laffitte agreed on 4 November 1825 to underwrite it at 80 percent of par, so that Haiti received about 24 million francs of the 30 million nominal. In 1833 Laffitte had a thousand of his own Haitian bonds reimbursed at full face value.

facts.claim: A 2022 Boston University Law Review article records that on 4 November 1825 Haiti and Laffitte's syndicate reached an agreement under which the 30-million-franc loan was to be underwritten at 80 percent of par.
facts.quote: On November 4, 1825, Haiti and Laffitte's syndicate reached an agreement. The loan was to be underwritten at 80% of par by a syndicate led by Laffitte

sources.title: A Debt of Dishonor

facts.claim: In early October 1825 the Paris bank Ternaux et Gandolphe prepared the documents for a projected 30-million-franc loan for Haiti repayable over 25 years, and a tender was launched to find the bank or group of bankers offering the best price for 30,000 bonds of 1,000 francs.
facts.quote: Un appel d'offre fut lancé dans le but de trouver une banque (ou un groupe de banquiers)

sources.title: Haïti / L'emprunt en 1825 de 30 millions de francs sur le marché des obligations à la Bourse de Paris et son remboursement
Neocolonialism through Debt: How French and U.S. Banks Underdeveloped Haiti

facts.claim: French accounts describe the 1825 operation as orchestrated by Jacques Laffitte with the baron Mallet and Denis-Charles Delessert, and name a consortium around Laffitte, the bank of Pierre-François Paravey and Rothschild Frères.
facts.quote: L'opération, orchestrée par Jacques Laffitte, le baron Mallet et Denis-Charles Delessert

facts.claim: Of the 30 million francs borrowed, Haiti received only 24 million, the commission amounting to 6 million francs.
facts.quote: Sur les 30 millions empruntés, Haïti n'en touche que 24, la commission s'élevant à 6 millions de francs.

sources.title: Haïti : Il y a 196 ans, la « dette de l'indépendance »

facts.claim: The same law review article says the banker Ternaux, an enthusiastic defender of the loan, claimed Haiti's annual revenues were around 37 million francs, a figure the authors call divorced from reality.
facts.quote: Ternaux, an enthusiastic defender of the loan, claimed that Haiti's annual revenues were in the region of 37 million francs, a figure divorced from reality.

facts.claim: In 1833 Laffitte had a thousand of his own Haitian bonds reimbursed by the Haitian government at their full face value, receiving one million francs for bonds he had bought for roughly 800,000.
facts.quote: in 1833 Jacques Laffitte had a thousand of his own Haitian bonds reimbursed by the Haitian government at their full face value

facts.claim: The 1825 loan, capital and interest, was repaid between 1826 and 1893; Haiti suspended payments on the 'double debt' from 1828.
facts.quote: Cet emprunt (capital et intérêts) fut remboursé de 1826 à 1893.

openQuestions: Site claim tested: 'a Laffitte-led consortium bought the bonds at 80% of face value and paid only 24M francs into the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations' — the 80 percent underwriting and the 24 million net are supported; the payment into the Caisse des Dépôts was not confirmed in the sources opened.
Site claim tested: that the loan was 'through Ternaux Gandolphe' — supported (Ternaux et Gandolphe prepared the loan and ran the tender).
No Gallica document was returned by the searches; the primary 1825 loan contract was not opened.
The attribution of the sentence naming Mallet and Delessert, and of the Paravey/Rothschild consortium, to the FME note versus Karibinfo could not be separated in the search listing; both are cited.
Sources conflict on the loan's interest rate (zero versus 6 percent); not recorded.
